title: Ἡ μάχη ἐν μεγάροις
titleEn: The Fight in the Hall — Odyssey 22.195–291
about: Eumaeus finishes taunting the bound goatherd Melanthius, and he and the cowherd arm and join Odysseus on the threshold. Athena arrives in the shape of Mentor, and Odysseus appeals to her as an old friend, half suspecting who she is. Agelaus warns the false Mentor not to take Odysseus's side and threatens her household; Athena, angered, rebukes Odysseus for no longer fighting as he did at Troy, then withholds the victory still and perches in the rafters as a swallow. Agelaus names six suitors to throw first, and Athena turns their spears aside. Odysseus and his three kill four of the suitors with one volley; the suitors throw again, and Telemachus and Eumaeus are grazed. In the next exchange Odysseus, Telemachus and the swineherd hit three more suitors, and the herdsman of the cattle strikes Ctesippus in the chest and mocks him with the foot he once threw at the beggar.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν δὴ μάλα πάγχυ, Μελάνθιε, νύκτα φυλάξεις,
εὐνῇ ἔνι μαλακῇ καταλέγμενος, ὥς σε ἔοικεν·
sentences.l:
“Now indeed, quite entirely, Melanthius, the night you will watch through,
lying in a soft bed, as it is fitting for you;
sentences.i: “Now, Melanthius, you will keep watch all night long, lying in a soft bed, as is fitting for you;
sentences.n: These are Eumaeus's words to Melanthius, the goatherd he has just bound and hauled up; the speech was introduced by the last line of the previous part (22.194), so the part opens inside it. The soft bed is irony. νύκτα φυλάξεις is 'you will keep watch through the night': νύκτα is an accusative of the time through which, and φυλάξεις the future of φυλάσσω. νῦν μὲν δὴ μάλα πάγχυ is 'now indeed, quite entirely': νῦν is the adverb 'now' and the rest is a pile of intensifying particles and adverbs. καταλέγμενος is a syncopated aorist middle participle of καταλέγω 'lie down', and ἔνι is ἐνί 'in', accented on the first syllable because it follows its noun εὐνῇ. ὥς σε ἔοικεν is 'as it is fitting for you', ἔοικε being impersonal.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ σέ γ’ ἠριγένεια παρ’ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων
λήσει ἐπερχομένη χρυσόθρονος, ἡνίκ’ ἀγινεῖς
αἶγας μνηστήρεσσι δόμον κάτα δαῖτα πένεσθαι.
sentences.l:
nor you, at least, early-born, from the streams of Oceanus
will she escape, coming, golden-throned, when you drive
goats for the suitors, down the house, a feast to prepare.”
sentences.i: and as early-born, golden-throned Dawn comes up from the streams of Oceanus, she will not escape your notice, at the hour when you drive goats to the suitors to prepare a feast in the house.”
sentences.n: Dawn is not named: her two stock epithets, ἠριγένεια 'early-born' and χρυσόθρονος 'golden-throned', stand alone for her and are translated as in the house table. οὐδέ σέ γε ... λήσει is 'nor will she escape you': λανθάνω takes the accusative of the person who does not notice, so the sense is that Melanthius will be awake, and see her coming, at dawn. ἐπερχομένη is the participle 'as she comes'. παρ’ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων is 'from beside the streams of Oceanus', the river thought to lie round the edge of the world, with the genitive plural ῥοάων for Attic ῥοῶν. ἀγινεῖς is 'you drive', from ἀγινέω, a longer form of ἄγω. δόμον κάτα is κατὰ δόμον 'down through the house', the preposition accented on the first syllable because it follows its noun. πένεσθαι is the infinitive of πένομαι 'toil at, prepare'.

sentences.t: ὣς ὁ μὲν αὖθι λέλειπτο, ταθεὶς ὀλοῷ ἐνὶ δεσμῷ·
sentences.l: So he indeed in that very place had been left behind, stretched in a deadly bond;
sentences.i: So he was left there, stretched out in his deadly bonds;
sentences.n: ὣς with a circumflex is the adverb 'so, thus', not the conjunction ὡς. ὁ μέν 'he, for his part' is set against τὼ δέ 'but the two' in the next line. λέλειπτο is the pluperfect passive of λείπω, 'had been left', without augment, and ταθείς the aorist passive participle of τείνω 'stretch'. ὀλοῷ ἐνὶ δεσμῷ is 'in a deadly bond', ἐνί being ἐν; ὀλοός 'destroying, deadly' is not the same word as ὅλος 'whole'. αὖθι is 'there, on the spot', with the place-suffix -θι.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἐς τεύχεα δύντε, θύρην ἐπιθέντε φαεινήν,
βήτην εἰς Ὀδυσῆα δαΐφρονα, ποικιλομήτην.
sentences.l:
and the two, into their armour having got, the shining door having shut to,
went to Odysseus, wise-minded, of many-colored cunning.
sentences.i: and the two of them, having put on their armour and shut the shining door, went to Odysseus, wise-hearted and full of shifting cunning.
sentences.n: τὼ is the dual 'the two', that is the swineherd and the cowherd who bound Melanthius; the dual endings in δύντε, ἐπιθέντε and βήτην all belong to it. δύντε is the aorist participle of δύω, here 'having got into' the armour, and ἐπιθέντε the aorist participle of ἐπιτίθημι 'put to, shut'. βήτην is the dual aorist of βαίνω, without augment. The two epithets of Odysseus are kept apart as in the house table: δαΐφρονα 'wise-minded' (its meaning is doubtful: from δαῆναι 'to know', or from δάϊος 'hostile') and ποικιλομήτην 'of many-colored cunning', from ποικίλος 'many-colored' and μῆτις 'cunning'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μένος πνείοντες ἐφέστασαν, οἱ μὲν ἐπ’ οὐδοῦ
τέσσαρες, οἱ δ’ ἔντοσθε δόμων πολέες τε καὶ ἐσθλοί.
sentences.l:
There, breathing strength, they took their stand, some on the threshold,
four, and others inside the house, many and good.
sentences.i: There they stood, breathing strength: on the threshold the four, and inside the house the others, many and good.
sentences.n: The two parties are set against each other by οἱ μέν ... οἱ δέ 'some ... others': the four on the threshold are Odysseus, Telemachus and the two herdsmen, and the many inside are the suitors. ἐφέστασαν is a past tense of ἐφίστημι, here without a direct object, 'took their stand'. μένος πνείοντες is 'breathing strength', a formula for fighting spirit; the house renders μένος as 'strength' and keeps 'might' for ἀλκή. ἔντοσθε is 'inside', with the genitive δόμων, and πολέες is the epic plural of πολύς, beside πολλοί. ἐσθλοί is 'good', as everywhere in the house table, said here of the suitors as fighters.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἐπ’ ἀγχίμολον θυγάτηρ Διὸς ἦλθεν Ἀθήνη,
Μέντορι εἰδομένη ἠμὲν δέμας ἠδὲ καὶ αὐδήν.
sentences.l:
And to them near at hand came the daughter of Zeus, Athena,
likened to Mentor, both in body and in voice.
sentences.i: And close to them came Athena, the daughter of Zeus, having taken the shape of Mentor, in body and in voice alike.
sentences.n: τοῖσι is 'to them', the four on the threshold, and ἐπ’ ... ἦλθεν is tmesis for ἐπῆλθεν 'came up'; ἀγχίμολον is an adverb 'close at hand'. Line 206 is word for word the line that stood at 2.268, and keeps its English there: Μέντορι εἰδομένη is 'made like Mentor' (εἰδομένη is the participle of εἴδομαι 'make oneself like', with the dative of likeness), and ἠμὲν δέμας ἠδὲ καὶ αὐδήν is 'both in body and in voice', two accusatives of respect after the epic pair ἠμέν ... ἠδέ 'both ... and'. Athena is the goddess to the narrator and to us; to the suitors she is Mentor.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς γήθησεν ἰδὼν καὶ μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.l: And at her Odysseus rejoiced, seeing her, and uttered a speech:
sentences.i: Odysseus was glad when he saw her, and spoke:
sentences.n: τὴν is 'her', the object of ἰδών. γήθησεν is the aorist of γηθέω 'rejoice', and ἔειπε is the longer Homeric form of εἶπε 'said'. μῦθον ἔειπε 'uttered a speech' is the half-line speech introduction rendered in the house table as 'and uttered a speech' (literal layer), 'and spoke' (idiomatic layer). Odysseus is glad because he sees a friend, as the next lines show; the speech follows.

sentences.t:
Μέντορ, ἄμυνον ἀρήν, μνῆσαι δ’ ἑτάροιο φίλοιο,
ὅς σ’ ἀγαθὰ ῥέζεσκον· ὁμηλικίην δέ μοί ἐσσι.
sentences.l:
“Mentor, ward off ruin, and remember a dear comrade,
who used to do you good things; and in equal age to me you are.”
sentences.i: “Mentor, ward off ruin, and remember a dear companion, who did you good again and again; and you are of an age with me.”
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks to Athena under the name Mentor. ἄμυνον ἀρήν is 'ward off ruin': ἀρή here means 'harm, bane', a different word from the ἀρή that means 'prayer'. μνῆσαι is the aorist imperative middle of μιμνήσκω 'remember', and takes the genitive ἑτάροιο φίλοιο 'a dear comrade', with the genitive in -οιο. The comrade is Odysseus himself, and so the relative clause ὅς σ’ ἀγαθὰ ῥέζεσκον changes person: the verb is first person, 'who used to do you good', ῥέζεσκον being the iterative imperfect of ῥέζω 'do', which shows repeated action. ὁμηλικίην is an accusative of respect, 'in sameness of age', so 'you are my age-mate'; ἐσσί is epic for εἶ 'you are', and μοί is 'to me'.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτ’, ὀϊόμενος λαοσσόον ἔμμεν Ἀθήνην.
sentences.l: So he spoke, supposing that it was Athena, the people-rousing.
sentences.i: So he spoke, supposing her to be Athena, rouser of the people.
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. The narrator tells us what Odysseus does not yet know: he speaks to Mentor, but guesses Athena. ὀϊόμενος is the participle of ὀΐομαι 'suppose, expect', the same verb as ὀΐω 'I suppose'. λαοσσόον is an epithet of Athena, 'rousing the people' if it comes from λαός 'people' and σεύω 'drive, rouse'; that derivation is disputed, and 'saving the people' was also ancient. The house renders it 'people-rousing' in the literal layer and 'rouser of the people' in the idiomatic, as for Amphiaraus. ἔμμεν is ἔμμεναι 'to be', and Ἀθήνην is the accusative subject of the infinitive: 'that it was Athena'. ὣς φάτ’ is 'so he spoke', φάτ’ being φάτο with its vowel elided.

sentences.t: μνηστῆρες δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ὁμόκλεον ἐν μεγάροισι·
sentences.l: and the suitors from the other side were shouting in the halls;
sentences.i: while on the other side the suitors were shouting in the halls;
sentences.n: ἑτέρωθεν is 'from the other side', with the suffix -θεν of 'from' (compare ἁμόθεν in the first part). ὁμόκλεον is the imperfect of ὁμοκλέω 'shout', without augment, and ἐν μεγάροισι is a dative plural in -οισι for the one hall of the house. The suitors have heard Odysseus speak to Mentor but not yet attacked.

sentences.t: πρῶτος τήν γ’ ἐνένιπε Δαμαστορίδης Ἀγέλαος·
sentences.l: first her rebuked Damastor's son Agelaus:
sentences.i: Agelaus, son of Damastor, was the first to rebuke her:
sentences.n: τήν is 'her': the narrator uses the feminine because he knows the speaker is a goddess, though Agelaus thinks he addresses a man. ἐνένιπε is the aorist of ἐνίπτω 'rebuke', with a reduplicated stem, and πρῶτος 'first' is in the nominative, agreeing with Agelaus: 'he first rebuked her'. Δαμαστορίδης is the patronymic 'son of Damastor', formed with -ίδης, and Ἀγέλαος is Homer's form of Agelaus.

sentences.t:
Μέντορ, μή σ’ ἐπέεσσι παραιπεπίθῃσιν Ὀδυσσεὺς
μνηστήρεσσι μάχεσθαι, ἀμυνέμεναι δέ οἱ αὐτῷ.
sentences.l:
“Mentor, let not Odysseus with words persuade you round
to fight against the suitors and to defend him himself.
sentences.i: “Mentor, do not let Odysseus talk you round with his words into fighting against the suitors and coming to his defence.
sentences.n: Agelaus addresses the false Mentor. μή with the aorist subjunctive παραιπεπίθῃσιν 'lest he persuade' is a warning; the verb is the reduplicated aorist subjunctive of παραπείθω 'win over, talk round', with the epic ending -ῃσιν for -ῃ. ἐπέεσσι is the dative plural 'with words' in -εσσι. μάχεσθαι takes the dative μνηστήρεσσι, 'fight against the suitors', and ἀμυνέμεναι is the epic infinitive in -έμεναι of ἀμύνω 'defend', with οἱ αὐτῷ 'for him himself'.

sentences.t: ὧδε γὰρ ἡμέτερόν γε νόον τελέεσθαι ὀΐω·
sentences.l: For thus our purpose, I suppose, will be accomplished:
sentences.i: For this is how I suppose our purpose will be fulfilled:
sentences.n: ὧδε 'thus' points forward to the two lines that follow. νόον is 'purpose, mind' (Attic νοῦν), the accusative subject of the infinitive τελέεσθαι, the uncontracted future middle infinitive of τελέω 'accomplish', with a passive sense: 'will be brought to pass'. ὀΐω is 'I suppose', as in the house table, and the particles γάρ and γε are 'for' and the emphatic 'at least'.

sentences.t:
ὁππότε κεν τούτους κτέωμεν, πατέρ’ ἠδὲ καὶ υἱόν,
ἐν δὲ σὺ τοῖσιν ἔπειτα πεφήσεαι, οἷα μενοινᾷς
ἔρδειν ἐν μεγάροις·
sentences.i: when we have killed these two, father and son, then you will be slain among them as well, for what you purpose to do in the halls;
sentences.n: ὁππότε κεν with the aorist subjunctive κτέωμεν is 'whenever we shall have killed', κεν being epic κε(ν), the particle for Attic ἄν; κτέωμεν is the aorist subjunctive of κτείνω in its epic uncontracted form. τούτους πατέρ’ ἠδὲ καὶ υἱόν are Odysseus and Telemachus. ἐν δὲ σὺ τοῖσιν ἔπειτα πεφήσεαι is 'and among them you will then be slain': ἐν ... τοῖσιν is 'among them', and πεφήσεαι the reduplicated future passive of φένω 'slay', with the uncontracted ending -εαι. οἷα μενοινᾷς ἔρδειν is 'for such things as you purpose to do', where οἷα is the cause and μενοινάω means 'purpose, intend' (here an ill intent); ἔρδειν is the epic infinitive of ἔρδω 'do'.

sentences.t: σῷ δ’ αὐτοῦ κράατι τίσεις.
sentences.l: and with your own head you will pay.
sentences.i: and you will pay the price with your own head.
sentences.n: σῷ ... κράατι is 'with your head', the dative of κάρη 'head' in the form κράατι (Attic κρατί); αὐτοῦ in σῷ δ’ αὐτοῦ is 'your very own'. τίσεις is the future of τίνω 'pay (a penalty)'. The phrase threatens death, as the line before has already said it.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν ὑμέων γε βίας ἀφελώμεθα χαλκῷ,
κτήμαθ’ ὁπόσσα τοί ἐστι, τά τ’ ἔνδοθι καὶ τὰ θύρηφι,
τοῖσιν Ὀδυσσῆος μεταμίξομεν·
sentences.i: And when we have taken away your strength with the bronze, all the possessions that are yours, within doors and outside, we shall mix in with those of Odysseus;
sentences.n: The address widens from Mentor to his party: ὑμέων is the genitive plural 'of you' (Attic ὑμῶν), where σοι and τοι elsewhere are singular. ἐπὴν ... ἀφελώμεθα is 'when we shall have taken away', the aorist subjunctive middle of ἀφαιρέω with ἐπήν 'when'; βίας is the accusative plural of βίη 'force, strength'. χαλκῷ is 'with bronze', the weapon. κτήματα is 'possessions', and τοί is the enclitic dative 'to you', so ὁπόσσα τοί ἐστι is 'as many as are yours'. τά τ’ ἔνδοθι καὶ τὰ θύρηφι 'both those within and those out of doors' has the suffixes -θι and -φι of place; here τά is a demonstrative. τοῖσιν Ὀδυσσῆος is 'with those of Odysseus', and μεταμίξομεν 'we shall mix in' is an epic future.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τοι υἷας
ζώειν ἐν μεγάροισιν ἐάσομεν, οὐδέ θύγατρας
οὐδ’ ἄλοχον κεδνὴν Ἰθάκης κατὰ ἄστυ πολεύειν.
sentences.l:
and not your sons
to live in the halls will we allow, nor your daughters,
nor your trusty wife in Ithaca's town to go about.”
sentences.i: and we will not let your sons live on in the halls, nor your daughters, nor your trusty wife go about the town of Ithaca.”
sentences.n: οὐδέ ... οὐδέ ... οὐδ’ is a run of three negatives, 'not ... nor ... nor', each attached to the objects of ἐάσομεν 'we shall allow': υἷας, θύγατρας, ἄλοχον. τοι is 'your', a dative of the person concerned. ζώειν is the uncontracted infinitive of ζάω 'live', and ἐν μεγάροισιν a dative plural in -οισιν. κεδνήν means 'trusty, careful', an epithet of a wife; the house translates κεδνός as 'trusty' every time. Ἰθάκης κατὰ ἄστυ is 'through the town of Ithaca', and πολεύειν the infinitive of πολεύω 'go about, range over'. Agelaus threatens to wipe out the family of the man he takes for Mentor.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτ’, Ἀθηναίη δὲ χολώσατο κηρόθι μᾶλλον,
νείκεσσεν δ’ Ὀδυσῆα χολωτοῖσιν ἐπέεσσιν·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Athena was angered in heart the more,
and she reviled Odysseus with angry words:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Athena grew still angrier in her heart, and she reviled Odysseus with angry words:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. χολώσατο is the aorist middle of χολόω 'make angry', 'became angry', and κηρόθι is 'in her heart', from κῆρ 'heart' with the suffix -θι. μᾶλλον 'the more' is a comparative adverb. νείκεσσεν is the aorist of νεικέω 'quarrel with, revile', in the form with doubled σ, which the house renders 'reviled'; δ’ gives 'and'. χολωτοῖσιν ἐπέεσσιν is 'with angry words', the house rendering of χολωτός as 'angry', a dative plural in -οισιν and -εσσιν. Athena is still in the shape of Mentor and now speaks to Odysseus as though she were the old Mentor chiding the old fighter.

sentences.t:
οὐκέτι σοί γ’, Ὀδυσεῦ, μένος ἔμπεδον οὐδέ τις ἀλκή
οἵη ὅτ’ ἀμφ’ Ἑλένῃ λευκωλένῳ εὐπατερείῃ,
εἰνάετες Τρώεσσιν ἐμάρναο νωλεμὲς αἰεί,
sentences.l:
“No longer in you, Odysseus, is there firm strength nor any might
such as when, around Helen, white-armed, of a noble father,
nine years with the Trojans you fought unceasingly always,
sentences.i: “Odysseus, you no longer have firm strength or any might such as you had when, for white-armed Helen, daughter of a noble father, you fought the Trojans for nine years, unceasingly and always,
sentences.n: Athena speaks, in Mentor's shape. σοί γε is 'in you at least', with σοι the dative of possession, and the particle γε singles Odysseus out. ἔμπεδον 'firm, steady' is the neuter agreeing with μένος, which the house renders 'strength', and ἀλκή is 'might'. οἵη 'such as' is feminine to agree with ἀλκή. ἀμφ’ Ἑλένῃ is 'around Helen', that is 'about Helen' as the prize; λευκωλένῳ 'white-armed' and εὐπατερείῃ 'of a noble father' (ἐύς 'good' and πατήρ) are datives agreeing with Ἑλένῃ. εἰνάετες is 'nine years long', used as an adverb, and ἐμάρναο is the imperfect middle of μάρναμαι 'fight', in the uncontracted form. νωλεμές 'unceasingly' and αἰεί 'always' are two words for the same point.

sentences.t:
πολλοὺς δ’ ἄνδρας ἔπεφνες ἐν αἰνῇ δηϊοτῆτι,
σῇ δ’ ἥλω βουλῇ Πριάμου πόλις εὐρυάγυια.
sentences.l:
and many men you killed in fearsome fighting,
and by your counsel was taken Priam's city, of the wide streets.
sentences.i: and killed many men in fearsome fighting, and by your counsel Priam's city of the wide streets was taken.
sentences.n: ἔπεφνες is the aorist of φένω 'slay', with the reduplicated stem (compare πεφήσεαι above). δηϊοτής is 'hostile fighting', a word for the clash of battle; αἰνῇ is 'fearsome' as in the house table. σῇ ... βουλῇ is 'by your counsel', a dative of means, and ἥλω is the Homeric aorist of ἁλίσκομαι 'be taken' (Attic ἑάλω). Πριάμου πόλις εὐρυάγυια is 'Priam's city of the wide streets': εὐρυάγυια is a compound of εὐρύς 'wide' and ἀγυιά 'street', rendered as in the house table.

sentences.t:
πῶς δὴ νῦν, ὅτε σόν τε δόμον καὶ κτήμαθ’ ἱκάνεις,
ἄντα μνηστήρων ὀλοφύρεαι ἄλκιμος εἶναι;
sentences.l:
How then now, when to your house and possessions you have come,
before the suitors do you lament to be valiant?
sentences.i: How is it, then, that now, when you have come to your own house and possessions, you lament at having to be valiant in the face of the suitors?
sentences.n: The Greek question mark ; ends the unit. πῶς δὴ νῦν is 'how then now'. ὅτε ... ἱκάνεις is 'when you have come', ἱκάνω being a longer form of ἱκνέομαι 'reach, come to', with the accusatives σὸν δόμον and κτήμαθ’ (κτήματα). ἄντα μνηστήρων is 'in front of the suitors', ἄντα with the genitive. ὀλοφύρεαι ἄλκιμος εἶναι is hard to put into English: ὀλοφύρομαι is 'lament, wail', and the infinitive εἶναι with ἄλκιμος 'valiant' is 'to be valiant'; the sense is that Odysseus laments when he should be showing valour, or that he bewails the need for it. ὀλοφύρεαι is an uncontracted second singular.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δεῦρο, πέπον, παρ’ ἔμ’ ἵστασο καὶ ἴδε ἔργον,
ὄφρ’ εἰδῇς οἷός τοι ἐν ἀνδράσι δυσμενέεσσιν
Μέντωρ Ἀλκιμίδης εὐεργεσίας ἀποτίνειν.
sentences.l:
But come, here, good one, stand beside me and see the deed,
that you may know what sort to you among hostile men
Mentor, son of Alcimus, is at repaying good deeds.”
sentences.i: But come here, my good fellow, stand beside me and watch what I do, so that you may know what kind of man Mentor, son of Alcimus, proves to be, among hostile men, in repaying good deeds to you.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come', and δεῦρο 'hither'. πέπον is a vocative of friendly address, here 'good one', house 'my good fellow'. ἵστασο is the present imperative middle of ἵστημι 'take your stand', and ἴδε the aorist imperative of εἶδον 'see', with ἔργον 'deed, work'. ὄφρ’ εἰδῇς is 'in order that you may know', the subjunctive of οἶδα. οἷός τοι ... Μέντωρ Ἀλκιμίδης is 'what sort of man to you Mentor, son of Alcimus, is'; Ἀλκιμίδης is the patronymic in -ίδης. Athena, still speaking as Mentor, gives Mentor a father's name. δυσμενέεσσιν is 'hostile', a dative plural in -εσσιν. εὐεργεσίας is 'good deeds', and ἀποτίνειν 'to pay back', the infinitive after οἷος.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ οὔ πω πάγχυ δίδου ἑτεραλκέα νίκην,
ἀλλ’ ἔτ’ ἄρα σθένεός τε καὶ ἀλκῆς πειρήτιζεν
ἠμὲν Ὀδυσσῆος ἠδ’ υἱοῦ κυδαλίμοιο.
sentences.l:
She spoke, and not yet altogether was giving the victory of strength-to-the-other-side,
but still she was testing the strength and the might
both of Odysseus and of his son, glorious.
sentences.i: So she said, but she did not yet grant a victory that would tip the balance; she went on testing the strength and the might of Odysseus and of his glorious son.
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. ἦ ῥα is 'she spoke' in the house table, a speech-closing formula. οὔ πω πάγχυ δίδου is 'not yet altogether was giving', δίδου being the imperfect of δίδωμι. ἑτεραλκέα νίκην 'a victory of strength to the other side' is a victory that gives the strength to one side or the other, a decisive one; the sense of ἑτεραλκής (ἕτερος 'the other' and ἀλκή) is disputed, and this is the traditional reading. πειρήτιζεν is the imperfect of πειρητίζω 'test, put to the proof', with the genitives σθένεος 'strength' and ἀλκῆς 'might'. ἠμὲν ... ἠδ’ is 'both ... and', as at 206. κυδαλίμοιο is 'glorious', from κῦδος 'glory', a genitive in -οιο. Athena keeps the fight in the balance to test them. Line 238 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the short, closed final syllable of Ὀδυσσῆος has to be read long before the vowel of ἠδ’, in the third foot.

sentences.t:
αὐτὴ δ’ αἰθαλόεντος ἀνὰ μεγάροιο μέλαθρον
ἕζετ’ ἀναΐξασα, χελιδόνι εἰκέλη ἄντην.
sentences.l:
and herself up the sooty hall's rafter
she sat, having darted up, like a swallow, face to face.
sentences.i: and she herself darted up and sat on the rafter of the soot-blackened hall, in the likeness of a swallow, in full view.
sentences.n: αὐτή 'she herself' is the goddess, who leaves the form of Mentor. αἰθαλόεντος is 'sooty', from αἴθαλος 'soot', agreeing with μεγάροιο, and μέλαθρον is 'roof-beam', also used for 'roof'; ἀνὰ ... μέλαθρον is 'up to the beam'. ἕζετ’ is the imperfect ἕζετο of ἕζομαι 'sat down', elided, and ἀναΐξασα the aorist participle of ἀναΐσσω 'dart up'. χελιδόνι εἰκέλη is 'like a swallow', εἰκέλη taking the dative. ἄντην is 'face to face, in full view'; its exact force here is not certain.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρας δ’ ὤτρυνε Δαμαστορίδης Ἀγέλαος,
Εὐρύνομός τε καὶ Ἀμφιμέδων Δημοπτόλεμός τε,
Πείσανδρός τε Πολυκτορίδης Πόλυβός τε δαΐφρων·
sentences.i: Agelaus, son of Damastor, urged on the suitors, and Eurynomus, Amphimedon, Demoptolemus, Peisander son of Polyctor, and Polybus the wise-hearted with him;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. ὤτρυνε is the aorist of ὀτρύνω 'urge on', in the singular because it agrees with the first of six subjects, Agelaus; the other five names follow in the nominative. Πολυκτορίδης is the patronymic 'son of Polyctor', and Δαμαστορίδης 'son of Damastor'. The name Πείσανδρος is the one who is killed at 268. δαΐφρων is the epithet shared with Odysseus, rendered 'wise-minded' in the literal layer and 'wise-hearted' in the idiomatic one by the house table; the meaning of the word is doubtful, so the epithet may say less about the suitor than the translation suggests.

sentences.t:
οἱ γὰρ μνηστήρων ἀρετῇ ἔσαν ἔξοχ’ ἄριστοι,
ὅσσοι ἔτ’ ἔζωον περί τε ψυχέων ἐμάχοντο·
sentences.l:
for these among the suitors in excellence were by far the best,
as many as were still alive and were fighting for their lives;
sentences.i: for these were by far the best of the suitors in excellence, of those who were still alive and fighting for their lives;
sentences.n: οἱ is 'these', the six named, and γάρ 'for' explains why they are the ones urged on. ἀρετῇ is a dative of respect, 'in excellence' (manly worth), and ἔσαν is ἦσαν 'were'; ἔξοχ’ ἄριστοι is 'by far the best'. ὅσσοι ... ἔζωον is 'as many as were still alive', ἔζωον being the uncontracted imperfect of ζάω. περὶ ψυχέων ἐμάχοντο is 'fought for their lives', the genitive plural ψυχέων with περί 'about, for the sake of'. The ano teleia closes the unit.

sentences.t: τοὺς δ’ ἤδη ἐδάμασσε βιὸς καὶ ταρφέες ἰοί.
sentences.l: but those already had overpowered the bow and the thick arrows.
sentences.i: The others had already been laid low by the bow and the arrows that came so thick.
sentences.n: τοὺς δ’ is 'but those', the other suitors, who have fallen in the earlier shooting. ἐδάμασσε is the aorist of δαμάζω 'overpower, kill', singular because it stands next to its subjects βιός 'bow' and the arrows (ἰοί, 'arrows'); βιός 'bow' is accented differently from βίος 'life'. ταρφέες is 'thick, close-packed'.

sentences.t: τοῖς δ’ Ἀγέλεως μετέειπεν, ἔπος πάντεσσι πιφαύσκων·
sentences.l: And among them Agelaus spoke, making known a word to all:
sentences.i: Then Agelaus spoke among them, making his word known to all:
sentences.n: This line is the same as the line at 22.131 and has the same English. μετέειπεν is 'spoke among', from μετά and εἶπον, and ἔπος πάντεσσι πιφαύσκων 'making known a word to all' uses the participle of πιφαύσκω with the dative πάντεσσι in -εσσι. The speech follows.

sentences.t: ὦ φίλοι, ἤδη σχήσει ἀνὴρ ὅδε χεῖρας ἀάπτους·
sentences.l: “Friends, soon this man will hold back his hands, untouchable;
sentences.i: “Friends, this man will soon stay his hands, irresistible as they were;
sentences.n: Agelaus speaks again, now to all the suitors. ἤδη is 'now, soon', and σχήσει is the future of ἔχω, 'will hold back', so ἀνὴρ ὅδε σχήσει χεῖρας is 'this man will check his hands', the object being χεῖρας. ἀάπτους is an epithet whose meaning is not known: 'untouchable' and 'irresistible' are both traditional guesses, and the house gives the first in the literal layer and the second in the idiomatic. ἀνήρ ὅδε is 'this man', Odysseus.

sentences.t:
καὶ δή οἱ Μέντωρ μὲν ἔβη κενὰ εὔγματα εἰπών,
οἱ δ’ οἶοι λείπονται ἐπὶ πρώτῃσι θύρῃσι.
sentences.l:
and now for him Mentor has gone, empty boasts having spoken,
and they alone are left at the foremost doors.
sentences.i: And now Mentor has gone and left him, after speaking empty boasts, and they are left alone at the front doors.
sentences.n: καὶ δή is 'and now'. οἱ is the dative 'for him', Odysseus, so 'Mentor has left him'. ἔβη is the aorist of βαίνω, 'went', here in the sense 'has gone away', and κενὰ εὔγματα εἰπών is 'having spoken empty boasts', where εὔγματα are 'boasts'. οἱ δ’ οἶοι are 'but they alone', Odysseus and his party, and λείπονται the present passive of λείπω, 'are left behind'. ἐπὶ πρώτῃσι θύρῃσι is 'at the foremost doors', a dative plural in -ῃσι. The suitors do not see that Mentor has become a swallow.

sentences.t:
τῷ νῦν μὴ ἅμα πάντες ἐφίετε δούρατα μακρά,
ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ οἱ ἓξ πρῶτον ἀκοντίσατ’, αἴ κέ ποθι Ζεὺς
δώῃ Ὀδυσσῆα βλῆσθαι καὶ κῦδος ἀρέσθαι.
sentences.l:
Therefore now do not all together let fly your long spears,
but come, you six first hurl, if perhaps Zeus
may grant that Odysseus be struck and that we win glory.
sentences.i: So now do not all hurl your long spears at once, but come, you six hurl first, in case Zeus may grant that Odysseus be hit and that we win glory.
sentences.n: τῷ is 'therefore'. μὴ ... ἐφίετε is 'do not let fly at', the present imperative of ἐφίημι; ἅμα πάντες is 'all at once'. ἄγεθ’ is the plural of ἄγε 'come', and οἱ ἕξ is 'you six' (οἱ the article as pronoun, ἕξ 'six'); ἀκοντίσατ’ is the aorist imperative of ἀκοντίζω 'hurl a javelin'. αἴ κε with the subjunctive δώῃ is 'in case he may grant', and ποθι is 'somewhere, perhaps'. Ὀδυσσῆα βλῆσθαι is 'that Odysseus be struck', βλῆσθαι the aorist passive infinitive in epic form of βάλλω, and κῦδος ἀρέσθαι 'to win glory', ἀρέσθαι the aorist middle infinitive of ἄρνυμαι 'win, gain'.

sentences.t: τῶν δ’ ἄλλων οὐ κῆδος, ἐπὴν οὗτός γε πέσῃσιν.
sentences.l: Of the others there is no concern, once this man at least has fallen.”
sentences.i: The rest will not matter, once this man has fallen.”
sentences.n: τῶν δ’ ἄλλων is 'but of the others' (genitive), and κῆδος 'concern, care' is the singular of κήδεα, which the house renders 'sorrows'; here the sense is the milder 'concern', and the clause means that the rest will not matter. ἐπήν with the aorist subjunctive πέσῃσιν is 'once he has fallen', πέσῃσιν having the ending -σιν, and οὗτός γε 'this man at least' picks out Odysseus again.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκόντισαν ὡς ἐκέλευεν,
ἱέμενοι·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they all then hurled their spears as he bade,
eager;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all hurled their spears as he had ordered, in their eagerness;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. ὣς ἔφαθ’ 'so he spoke' is the ordinary closing formula (ἔφατο with the vowel elided), and οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες 'and they all then' begins the action. ἀκόντισαν is the aorist of ἀκοντίζω 'hurl a javelin', and ὡς ἐκέλευεν is 'as he ordered'. ἱέμενοι is the participle of ἵεμαι 'press forward, be eager', as at 1.6, in the house rendering 'eager'.

sentences.t:
τὰ δὲ πάντα ἐτώσια θῆκεν Ἀθήνη,
τῶν ἄλλος μὲν σταθμὸν ἐϋσταθέος μεγάροιο
βεβλήκει, ἄλλος δὲ θύρην πυκινῶς ἀραρυῖαν·
sentences.i: but Athena made all of them useless: one man struck the doorpost of the sturdy hall, another the tightly fitted door;
sentences.n: τά is 'those' (the spears), and ἐτώσια θῆκεν is 'made useless', ἐτώσιος meaning 'idle, to no purpose'. The next two lines are repeated at 274–275 and the English is the same there. ἄλλος μέν ... ἄλλος δέ is 'one ... another', and the pluperfect βεβλήκει 'had hit' stands for a simple past. σταθμός is 'doorpost'. ἐϋσταθέος 'well-standing, firmly set' is genitive with μεγάροιο, and πυκινῶς ἀραρυῖαν is 'closely fitted', ἀραρυῖα being the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω 'fit together'. Athena's work is the reason the spears miss.

sentences.t: ἄλλου δ’ ἐν τοίχῳ μελίη πέσε χαλκοβάρεια.
sentences.l: and of another in the wall the ash-spear fell, bronze-heavy.
sentences.i: and in the wall a third man's bronze-weighted ash spear fell.
sentences.n: ἄλλου is the genitive of ἄλλος, 'and of another', the third in the list; it depends on μελίη 'ash spear' (the shaft is made of ash, and the word stands for the spear). χαλκοβάρεια is 'heavy with bronze', feminine of an adjective in -ης agreeing with μελίη. τοίχῳ is 'wall' in the dative. The line comes again at 276.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ δούρατ’ ἀλεύαντο μνηστήρων,
τοῖς δ’ ἄρα μύθων ἦρχε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l:
But when they had avoided the spears of the suitors,
to them then the speeches began much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: But when they had dodged the suitors' spears, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus began to speak to them:
sentences.n: ἀλεύαντο is the aorist middle of ἀλέομαι 'avoid, dodge', and μνηστήρων is the genitive dependent on δούρατ’ (δούρατα, 'spears'). τοῖς is 'to them', his own side. μύθων ἦρχε is 'began the speeches', ἄρχω taking the genitive. πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is the standing name-phrase, 'much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus'; πολύτλας is nominative singular of a first-declension masculine.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, ἤδη μέν κεν ἐγὼν εἴποιμι καὶ ἄμμι
μνηστήρων ἐς ὅμιλον ἀκοντίσαι, οἳ μεμάασιν
ἡμέας ἐξεναρίξαι ἐπὶ προτέροισι κακοῖσιν.
sentences.l:
“Friends, now indeed I would say that we also
into the throng of the suitors should hurl, who are eager
to kill us, on top of their former evils.”
sentences.i: “Friends, I would now bid us too hurl our spears into the throng of the suitors, who are eager to kill us on top of their earlier wrongs.”
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. ἤδη μέν κεν ... εἴποιμι is 'I would now say', the potential optative with κεν, and the infinitive ἀκοντίσαι depends on it: 'I would say to throw', that is 'I would bid us throw'. ἄμμι is the Aeolic form of ἡμῖν 'to us', and καὶ ἄμμι 'to us also' means 'we too'. ἐς ὅμιλον is 'into the throng', and οἳ μεμάασιν 'who are eager' uses the perfect μέμαα of μάω, with the infinitive ἐξεναρίξαι 'to kill and strip of arms'; ἡμέας is the uncontracted accusative plural of ἡμεῖς. ἐπὶ προτέροισι κακοῖσιν is 'in addition to their earlier evils', the dative plural in -οισιν.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκόντισαν ὀξέα δοῦρα
ἄντα τιτυσκόμενοι·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they all then hurled their sharp spears,
aiming straight at them;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all hurled their sharp spears, aiming straight at them;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκόντισαν is the same clause as at 255, up to ἀκόντισαν. ὀξέα δοῦρα is 'sharp spears', δοῦρα being the plural of δόρυ, and the house gives 'sharp' for ὀξύς as in ξίφος ὀξύ. ἄντα τιτυσκόμενοι is 'aiming straight at them', τιτύσκομαι meaning 'aim at, take aim'. The ano teleia ends the unit, with the names of the dead to come.

sentences.t:
Δημοπτόλεμον μὲν Ὀδυσσεύς,
Εὐρυάδην δ’ ἄρα Τηλέμαχος, Ἔλατον δὲ συβώτης,
Πείσανδρον δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπεφνε βοῶν ἐπιβουκόλος ἀνήρ.
sentences.l:
Demoptolemus Odysseus,
and Euryades Telemachus, and Elatus the swineherd,
and Peisander the man, the herdsman of the cattle, killed.
sentences.i: Demoptolemus fell to Odysseus, Euryades to Telemachus, Elatus to the swineherd, and Peisander to the herdsman of the cattle.
sentences.n: Each name has its killer set beside it, and a single verb, ἔπεφνε 'slew', at the end of the sentence serves all four; the English has to carry 'killed' over to each, and the translation does it by recasting the clause. Δημοπτόλεμον ... Ὀδυσσεύς is 'Odysseus killed Demoptolemus', with the object first, and Εὐρυάδην, Ἔλατον, Πείσανδρον are accusatives. συβώτης is 'swineherd', and βοῶν ἐπιβουκόλος ἀνήρ 'the man, the herdsman of the cattle' is the standing description of the cowherd, translated as in the earlier parts; ἐπί 'in charge of' and βουκόλος 'cowherd' make a herdsman set over cattle. Philoetius is the herdsman's name in the earlier parts, but the line does not use it.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἔπειθ’ ἅμα πάντες ὀδὰξ ἕλον ἄσπετον οὖδας,
μνηστῆρες δ’ ἀνεχώρησαν μεγάροιο μυχόνδε·
sentences.l:
They then all together with their teeth bit the boundless ground,
and the suitors drew back to the recess of the hall;
sentences.i: They all fell together and bit the boundless earth with their teeth, and the suitors drew back to the innermost part of the hall;
sentences.n: οἱ μέν are the four who have just been killed, and ἔπειθ’ 'then' is the elided ἔπειτα. ὀδὰξ ἕλον οὖδας is 'bit the ground with their teeth', an expression for dying on the ground; ἕλον is the aorist of αἱρέω and οὖδας 'ground' is the Homeric word for floor or earth; ἄσπετον is 'boundless, not to be told' (the earlier parts keep 'boundless'). ἀνεχώρησαν is the aorist of ἀναχωρέω 'withdraw', and μεγάροιο μυχόνδε 'to the recess of the hall' has the suffix -δε of direction, the genitive going with μυχόν. μνηστῆρες δ’ 'but the suitors' are the survivors.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπήϊξαν, νεκύων δ’ ἐξ ἔγχε’ ἕλοντο.
sentences.l: and they then rushed on, and from the dead their spears took out.
sentences.i: and the others rushed forward and pulled their spears out of the dead.
sentences.n: τοὶ is 'they', Odysseus and his side, the article as a pronoun and a contrast to μνηστῆρες. ἐπήϊξαν is the aorist of ἐπαΐσσω 'rush upon', and νεκύων ... ἐξ ... ἕλοντο is tmesis for ἐξείλοντο 'took out for themselves', with the middle voice showing that the spears are their own gain. ἔγχε’ is ἔγχεα 'spears', elided.

sentences.t:
αὖτις δὲ μνηστῆρες ἀκόντισαν ὀξέα δοῦρα
ἱέμενοι·
sentences.l:
And again the suitors hurled their sharp spears,
eager;
sentences.i: And again the suitors hurled their sharp spears, eager;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. αὖτις is 'again', and the line is the suitors' version of 265: ὀξέα δοῦρα 'sharp spears' as there. ἱέμενοι 'eager' is the participle also at 256. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 273.

sentences.t: τὰ δὲ πολλὰ ἐτώσια θῆκεν Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l: but the many of them to no purpose made Athena.
sentences.i: but Athena made most of them useless.
sentences.n: τὰ δὲ πολλά is 'but the many of them', that is most of the spears, where 256 had τὰ δὲ πάντα 'all of them'; the verb ἐτώσια θῆκεν 'made useless' is the same. The unit ends with a full stop in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
τῶν ἄλλος μὲν σταθμὸν ἐϋσταθέος μεγάροιο
βεβλήκειν, ἄλλος δὲ θύρην πυκινῶς ἀραρυῖαν·
sentences.l:
of them, one the doorpost of the well-standing hall
had struck, another the door, closely fitted;
sentences.i: one man struck the doorpost of the sturdy hall, another the tightly fitted door;
sentences.n: These two lines repeat 257–258, with βεβλήκειν for βεβλήκει (the same pluperfect 'had struck', with a final ν, or else the plural ending -ειν), and the English is the same, 'one ... another'. See the note there for σταθμός, ἐϋσταθέος and πυκινῶς ἀραρυῖαν. The ano teleia closes the unit.

sentences.t: ἄλλου δ’ ἐν τοίχῳ μελίη πέσε χαλκοβάρεια.
sentences.l: and of another in the wall the ash-spear fell, bronze-heavy.
sentences.i: and in the wall a third man's bronze-weighted ash spear fell.
sentences.n: This line is the same as 259 and has the same English.

sentences.t:
Ἀμφιμέδων δ’ ἄρα Τηλέμαχον βάλε χεῖρ’ ἐπὶ καρπῷ
λίγδην, ἄκρον δὲ ῥινὸν δηλήσατο χαλκός.
sentences.l:
And Amphimedon struck Telemachus on the hand at the wrist
grazingly, and the surface of the skin the bronze hurt.
sentences.i: Amphimedon hit Telemachus on the hand at the wrist, a glancing blow, and the bronze hurt only the outer skin.
sentences.n: Ἀμφιμέδων is the subject and Τηλέμαχον the object, so Amphimedon hits Telemachus; the name Amphimedon also stood in the list at 242. βάλε is the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω, and χεῖρ’ ἐπὶ καρπῷ 'on the hand at the wrist' puts the hand in the accusative and the wrist in the dative. λίγδην is 'grazing, scraping', an adverb. ἄκρον ῥινόν is 'the top of the skin', ῥινός being 'skin'; δηλήσατο is the aorist middle of δηλέομαι 'hurt, damage'. χαλκός 'bronze' is the spear's head.

sentences.t:
Κτήσιππος δ’ Εὔμαιον ὑπὲρ σάκος ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ
ὦμον ἐπέγραψεν·
sentences.l:
And Ctesippus, above the shield, with a long spear
grazed Eumaeus on the shoulder;
sentences.i: Ctesippus, over the top of the shield, grazed Eumaeus's shoulder with his long spear;
sentences.n: Κτήσιππος is the subject and Εὔμαιον the object. ὑπὲρ σάκος is 'over the shield', the house σάκος 'shield', and ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ is 'with a long spear', a dative. ὦμον is 'shoulder', accusative, and ἐπέγραψεν is the aorist of ἐπιγράφω 'scratch the surface of, graze'. The ano teleia closes the unit in the middle of line 280.

sentences.t: τὸ δ’ ὑπέρπτατο, πῖπτε δ’ ἔραζε.
sentences.l: and it flew over, and fell to the ground.
sentences.i: and the spear flew past above him and dropped to the ground.
sentences.n: τό is 'it', the spear, the article as a pronoun. ὑπέρπτατο is the aorist middle of ὑπερπέτομαι 'fly over', unaugmented. πῖπτε is the imperfect of πίπτω 'fall', and ἔραζε is 'to the ground', with the suffix -ζε of direction.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ αὖτ’ ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆα δαΐφρονα ποικιλομήτην,
μνηστήρων ἐς ὅμιλον ἀκόντισαν ὀξέα δοῦρα.
sentences.l:
And they in turn around Odysseus, wise-minded, of many-colored cunning,
into the throng of the suitors hurled their sharp spears.
sentences.i: And they in turn, about Odysseus, wise-hearted and full of shifting cunning, hurled their sharp spears into the throng of the suitors.
sentences.n: τοὶ δ’ αὖτ’ is 'and they in turn', Odysseus's side again after the suitors' throw. ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆα is 'about Odysseus', gathered round him. δαΐφρονα and ποικιλομήτην are the two separate epithets, as at 202. The line ends as 265 and 272 do: ὀξέα δοῦρα 'sharp spears'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ Εὐρυδάμαντα βάλε πτολίπορθος Ὀδυσσεύς,
Ἀμφιμέδοντα δὲ Τηλέμαχος, Πόλυβον δὲ συβώτης·
sentences.l:
Then in turn Eurydamas city-sacking Odysseus struck,
and Amphimedon Telemachus, and Polybus the swineherd;
sentences.i: Then in turn Eurydamas was hit by Odysseus, sacker of cities, Amphimedon by Telemachus, and Polybus by the swineherd;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ is 'then in turn'. Εὐρυδάμαντα is the object and πτολίπορθος Ὀδυσσεύς the subject: Odysseus hits Eurydamas, Telemachus hits Amphimedon (who grazed him at 277), and the swineherd hits Polybus. πτολίπορθος is 'sacker of cities' (πτόλις 'city' and πέρθω 'sack'), and πτολίπορθος Ὀδυσσεύς is the epithet and name together; the house gives 'city-sacking' in the literal layer. συβώτης is 'swineherd', the verb βάλε of the first clause serving all three.

sentences.t:
Κτήσιππον δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα βοῶν ἐπιβουκόλος ἀνὴρ
βεβλήκει πρὸς στῆθος, ἐπευχόμενος δὲ προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
and Ctesippus then the man, the herdsman of the cattle,
had struck on the chest, and, vaunting, addressed him:
sentences.i: and the herdsman of the cattle struck Ctesippus in the chest, and spoke to him in triumph:
sentences.n: The verb βάλε of 283 is understood for Telemachus and the swineherd in 284, and βεβλήκει 'had struck', the pluperfect used for a simple past, is the verb of the herdsman's blow. Κτήσιππον δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα 'and Ctesippus then' is the object, the same man who grazed Eumaeus at 279. βοῶν ἐπιβουκόλος ἀνήρ is the standing description of the cowherd (see 268). πρὸς στῆθος is 'in the chest'. ἐπευχόμενος is 'vaunting, boasting over' the victim, from ἐπεύχομαι; the same verb means 'pray' elsewhere, but here the participle is a boast made over a man just hit. προσηύδα is 'addressed', and the unit ends at the ano teleia that introduces the speech.

sentences.t:
ὦ Πολυθερσεΐδη φιλοκέρτομε, μή ποτε πάμπαν
εἴκων ἀφραδίῃς μέγα εἰπεῖν, ἀλλὰ θεοῖσιν
μῦθον ἐπιτρέψαι, ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτεροί εἰσι.
sentences.l:
“O son of Polytherses, taunt-loving, never at all
yielding to follies speak big, but to the gods
the word entrust, since in truth much stronger are they.
sentences.i: “Son of Polytherses, lover of taunts, never at all speak boastfully, yielding to folly, but leave the word to the gods, since in truth they are much stronger.
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. The herdsman of the cattle speaks to the dying Ctesippus. Πολυθερσεΐδη is the vocative of the patronymic 'son of Polytherses', and φιλοκέρτομε 'lover of taunts' is built on κερτομέω 'taunt', as at 194. The two infinitives εἰπεῖν and ἐπιτρέψαι stand for commands: μή ποτε ... εἰπεῖν is 'never speak' and the sense is 'do not say big things', while ἐπιτρέψαι is 'entrust', 'leave'. εἴκων is the participle of εἴκω 'yield', and ἀφραδίῃς is 'to follies', the dative plural of ἀφραδίη 'folly', the house rendering for the plural. μέγα εἰπεῖν is 'to speak big', that is 'to talk boastfully'. θεοῖσιν is 'to the gods', and φέρτεροι 'stronger, better' is comparative, with ἦ 'in truth' and πολύ 'much'.

sentences.t:
τοῦτό τοι ἀντὶ ποδὸς ξεινήϊον, ὅν ποτ’ ἔδωκας
ἀντιθέῳ Ὀδυσῆϊ δόμον κάτ’ ἀλητεύοντι.
sentences.l:
This is for you the guest-gift in return for the foot, which once you gave
to godlike Odysseus wandering through the house.”
sentences.i: This is your guest-gift in return for the foot, which you once gave to godlike Odysseus as he went wandering through the house.”
sentences.n: τοῦτό τοι is 'this to you', the spear that has just hit Ctesippus, given as a return gift. ἀντὶ ποδός is 'in exchange for the foot': the foot is the ox's foot that Ctesippus threw at Odysseus the beggar (20.299, in the earlier parts), and ξεινήϊον is 'guest-gift', the gift due to a guest, here turned into a blow. ὅν is the relative 'which', not the possessive, and being masculine it refers back to ποδός 'foot', not to the neuter ξεινήϊον; ὅν ποτ’ ἔδωκας is 'which you once gave'. ἀντιθέῳ Ὀδυσῆϊ is 'to godlike Odysseus', ἀντίθεος being 'godlike'. δόμον κάτ’ is κατὰ δόμον 'through the house', with the preposition after its noun, and ἀλητεύοντι is the dative participle of ἀλητεύω 'wander as a vagrant'.
